name: Wei Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a motor grader at a large mine, shaping the haul road so trucks do not bounce themselves apart. I am 58 with a vocational certificate, though reading drainage after rain took years to learn. I enjoy seeing a smooth camber in the mirror; the hard bit is a washout that has already stranded a truck. My partner works regular hours at a town library, our grown children live on their own, and we have saved about two months of expenses on typical mine pay. A few other mines are within driving distance, and I use an AI tool now and then to find manual sections after an experienced operator confirms the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew quicker paperwork sounds fine if nobody mistakes it for a repaired haul road. I would say road grading still needs a driver who can see where the rain runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours look safe in a small-change world, and the library wage helps cover our bills. I would still watch the equipment budget, because a delayed blade replacement can make every shift harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading the haul road and note blocked drains after rain. I'd ask the maintenance desk to replace the worn blade before the next wet season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the work in this version. We have two months of expenses saved, which gives us room for a normal repair, although I would like more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a worn blade change recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worn grader blade left ridges near the loading turn, and I had to make another pass. I took a photo for maintenance, then showed the fitter the edge in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the grader still needs someone in the seat and the library hours look steady. We would keep the two-month reserve for bills, not treat it as spare spending money.

He focuses on **blade wear and drainage**, practical work the plateau leaves in human hands.

steps.text: Keep grading the haul road and recording blocked drains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AI scheduling may move our calls around before any robot grades a road. I would ask the union for paid screen practice and a way to report mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer planners could make grader routes tighter, with less overtime to fix washouts. I will try the tool after others test it, but I want rain damage visible in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative to bring grader operators into the route-plan trial. I'd try the AI route screen during a paid shift after another operator demonstrates it. I'd record washout callouts against the new schedule for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy about being sent by a tidy map that missed a blocked drain. If the new schedule cuts paid callouts, our household income could fall, although the reserve gives us a little room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the trial to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the software's priority list with the drains we clear after a hard shower. If it sends me to a dry stretch first, somebody needs to change the data. A tidy map can miss a blocked drain that fills the haul road after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would lost callouts mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The base wage and my partner's library pay would still cover our regular bills. We would save less for retirement and delay replacing the old fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2028 can plan roads, with capable grader robots coming around 2031. I would ask the union for paid transitions before the mine buys a driverless grader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a robot grader in 2031 to threaten my wage, not just the planning office. Our two-month reserve would go quickly if both mine work and local vacancies shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine manager when grader robots will be tested on the haul roads. I'd apply for drainage inspection work at another site if a paid post opens. I'd join the union's transition committee to press for paid retraining and notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed by the short gap between a clever plan and a machine that can drive the road. I lie awake thinking about the mortgage payment if the grader seat goes before I find another post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still grade the roads if the mine has human drivers, and check whether AI planning changes the daily route. I would visit the other site about a drainage post rather than assume my experience transfers automatically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the library wage carry the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's library pay would cover food and some utilities, not our full mortgage. We would need another paid job or a serious bridge while I trained.

fieldNote: He places **job danger in 2031**, when capable robots could grade, while planning changes earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes the route office while grader robots follow around 2034. I would tell the union three extra years should fund real inspection places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could move from the grader into checking drainage if the mine keeps my pay. By 66 in 2034, I may still need the wage, so a robot would still matter to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shadow the drainage inspector on a paid shift next spring. I'd enroll in the site inspection course if fees and wages are covered. I'd keep grading roads in 2032 while applying for inspection openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture trying the new work without leaving my wage behind. I would be anxious until I knew that the inspection jobs would exist beyond a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on that shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to see the culvert under the east crossing after a storm. A photograph from a dry morning cannot show where silt blocks the outlet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspector says there are no openings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the grader wage and ask the union to bring vacancy numbers to the next meeting. I would also watch the other mines, but I would not take an unpaid course on a guess.

fieldNote: His **culvert example** gives a concrete reason to test drainage inspection rather than rely on plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI may plan the roads while robot graders arrive around 2039. I would tell the crew ten years of warning should include honest wage and training figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I might still work part time if our retirement account is short. By 71 in 2039, I hope to be off the grader, but I cannot promise that with two months saved today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid grader work while the road and my health allow. I'd transfer overtime pay into a separate retirement account each month. I'd review mortgage and savings figures with my partner once a year before cutting hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning feels less urgent because the work should last for years. I am uneasy about what we can afford at 68, not expecting next year's income to vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2037, after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 69 and still take paid grader shifts if we need them, even if AI sets the route. Capable robots are not due until around 2039 in this picture, so I would use the time to check whether the retirement figures add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are making their own way and do not owe us a retirement plan. We might ask them to help sort the papers. Our grown children's wages stay out of our retirement calculation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a robot grader around 2031 could take my wage while we still owe on the house. Paid drainage training, real inspection vacancies and notice of robot tests would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask what happens when a route plan meets the first storm of the season. A blocked culvert is a small thing on a screen and a big thing under a haul truck.

portrait: Wei is a **58-year-old motor-grader operator** at a large mine, with a vocational certificate and typical pay.
His partner's regular library income and **two months saved** support bills, though a mortgage remains.
He uses **AI occasionally** and wants operator testing before relying on new route screens.
He seeks **paid drainage training** and union input while keeping retirement tied to mortgage figures.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because robot graders around 2031 could remove a wage needed for the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid drainage training**, inspection vacancies and clear notice of robot tests.
